analysis.one_liner: Creates a national health insurance program covering every resident with no copays or deductibles, funded by higher taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, received one hearing in June 1992, and died there when the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, and federal employee health coverage with a single national health insurance program run by the government. Every U.S. resident would be automatically enrolled and covered for hospital care, doctor visits, prescription drugs, dental, vision, nursing home care, mental health, and more — with no copays, deductibles, or coinsurance. It would be paid for by raising corporate income tax from 34% to 38%, raising income tax rates up to 38%, lifting the wage cap on hospital insurance taxes, and charging most seniors a $55 monthly premium.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident — including lawful resident aliens — would gain full health coverage with no out-of-pocket costs at the point of care. People who are uninsured or underinsured, families facing medical bills, seniors needing long-term care, and people with pre-existing conditions would gain the most, since coverage would be automatic and complete.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Every resident and lawful resident alien would be automatically enrolled at birth or immigration and issued a national health insurance card.

Covered benefits include hospital care, professional services, prescription drugs, dental care, vision care, nursing facility care, hospice, mental health care, substance abuse treatment, and home and community-based care.
The bill prohibits all coinsurance, deductibles, and copayments for covered services, and providers must accept the program's payment as payment in full — no balance billing.
Hospitals would be paid through annual approved budgets, and payment schedules would be designed to encourage doctors to practice in rural and medically underserved areas.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations (top rate rising from 34% to 38%), high-income households (new brackets reaching 38%), employers and self-employed people (hospital insurance tax raised to 7.5% with the wage cap removed), most seniors (a $55 monthly premium), and beneficiaries of Social Security (taxable portion raised from 50% to 85%).
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations, high earners, employers, most seniors

drawbacks.text: The financing falls partly on middle-income families: the new rate schedule imposes a 30% bracket starting at $32,450 for joint filers and a 34% bracket above $78,400, a substantial tax increase for ordinary households.
Most seniors would owe a new $55 monthly long-term care/health care premium, deducted from Social Security checks, unless their income is very low.

Total program spending would be capped at last year's spending plus growth in the gross national product, and hospitals would operate under government-approved annual budgets with profits limited to a fixed rate of return — cost controls that could constrain access or wait times.

Private insurance could only be sold for benefits not covered by the program, eliminating today's employer-based plans for covered care, and Medicare, Medicaid, CHAMPUS, and federal employee coverage would be terminated after 1994.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is enormous and universal: complete coverage with zero out-of-pocket costs, including services most plans today skip, like dental, vision, drugs, and long-term care. The cost is also real and broad-based — middle-income taxpayers, employers, and seniors would all pay more, not just the wealthy. The spending cap and global budgets are a serious good-faith concern: they control costs by limiting the total money in the system, which could mean slower access to some care. The bill gave itself under a year to transition from five overlapping programs to one, an unusually short runway for a change this large.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the Senate Finance Committee, got a single hearing in June 1992, and sat there until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993 — no markup, no floor vote, nothing in the House either.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Wellstone introduced the Universal Health Care Act of 1992 on March 5, 1992, with Senators Metzenbaum and Simon as the only cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which held hearings on June 17, 1992.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never voted it out, and the bill never reached the Senate floor or the House before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers keep their existing role insuring Americans, employers keep the current employer-based system, and corporations and high earners avoid the tax increases the bill would have imposed. The roughly 37 million Americans then without insurance did not gain coverage.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican ever supported the bill; since it never reached a floor vote, the record shows no measure of broader support on either side.

industries.note: The bill would end Medicare, Medicaid, CHAMPUS, and federal employee coverage and allow private insurance only for benefits the program does not cover, shrinking the industry to a thin supplemental market. Its gain under the status quo comes from premiums paid by ordinary people, so its loss would be the public's gain.

Hospitals would get guaranteed payment through government-approved annual budgets, but spending would be capped, capital spending would be budgeted centrally, and profits beyond a fixed rate of return would be barred. The industry's interest in keeping costs uncontrolled runs against patients' interest in affordable care.

Doctor and professional payments would be set by a government fee schedule on a relative-value scale, and providers must accept program payment as payment in full with no extra billing. Fee-for-service income at current rates would be constrained.

Prescription drugs would become a covered benefit for everyone, guaranteeing a large market, but the Health and Human Services Secretary would maintain an approved-drug list and could exclude 'ineffective, unsafe or overpriced products' where better alternatives exist.

Employers would pay a higher hospital insurance tax (7.5% with no wage cap) but would be relieved of providing and administering health benefits for workers under the terminated employer-based and Medicare systems.
The program would process claims through competitively bid contracts with qualified entities, a business line insurers and fiscal intermediaries could win.
